content:
Below is a 20‑minute “awareness‑training” pack you can copy‑paste into a slide deck, hand out, or present live.  
It stays realistic (no fictional email addresses), uses the exact details you shared (architecture firm, 25 staff, Winterthur), and keeps text short enough to fit a quick briefing.

────────────────────────────────────────  
A 20‑Minute Phishing Brief for Your Firm  
(Office Manager – Winterthur Architecture Firm, 25 people)

Slide 1 – Title  
“Phishing – What It Is & How to Spot It  
(25-min training – Friday, [Date])”

Slide 2 – What Is Phishing?  
• A cyber‑attack disguised as a legitimate request.  
• Goal: trick someone into giving login data, personal info, or bank details.  
• No malware is required; the attacker only needs one click (or a typed password).

Slide 3 – Real‑Life Example #1 – “Change your password”  
Signature Block:  
“Security @WinterthurArch via [fake email address]  
Wednesday 09:00 → https://fake-password-update.winterthurarch.ch  
*Must use new credentials – 10 min window*”

What to watch for:  
- Slight spelling mistake in the domain (replace “winterthurarch” with “winterthurarch.ch” or a misspelling).  
- Urgency (“10 min window”).  
- Call to action: “click this link and type your old password”.

Slide 4 – Real‑Life Example #2 – “Package delivery”  
Signature Block:  
“DHL Tracking – Your parcel is ready for pickup  
Click to see tracking → http://tracking.dhl.ch/winterthur/…  
[Urgent package – bill invoices inside]”

What to watch for:  
- Unexpected link from a courier that now includes “winterthur” to sound authentic.  
- Asking for “access code” or “verification number” in the log-in dialog.  
- A generic greeting (“Dear valued firm member”) instead of your usual client contact name.

Slide 5 – Typical Look‑Alike Vehicles  
• Fake security alerts (Windows Defender, McAfee).  
• Inside-sales “client contract”; needs you to “log in” to view.  
• Social‑email “CEO” asking transfer money.  
• Google / Amazon “account review” form.

Slide 6 – Red Flags Checklist (TL;DR)  
□ Unusual sender address  
□ Spelling/grammar mistakes (poor proofread)  
□ Unexpected request (password reset, money transfer, invoices)  
□ Link URL does not look like the official site (different top-level, extra path)  
□ Urgency (“now”, “before 5 min”, “action needed”)  
□ Form asks for password or OTP

Slide 7 – 60-Second Test  
1. Copy the short link from slide 3. Paste into your browser—notice the real winterthurarch.ch vs. fake info.  
2. Look only at the email address shown in the “From:” line—does it match what your staff usually see?

Slide 8 – What to Do If You Receive Suspicious Email  
1. Do NOT click links or type anything.  
2. Forward the email to the IT helpdesk at it-support@[firm-domain.ch].  
3. Delete the email from inbox and junk.  
4. No reply—don’t engage.

Slide 9 – Quick Recap  
1) Phishing = fake request masquerading as safe → steal credentials  
2) Red flags: misspellings, odd links, urgent tone, unexpected requests  
3) If you doubt an email—stop, forward, delete.  
Ask questions (2–3 min Q&A).

────────────────────────────────────────  
How to deliver  
• Start with 1 slide title.  
• Read aloud 2–3 bullets each and paste small real emails into the projector (you already have two real-world snippets; add a third generic example).  
• Spend 2 minutes on Checklist and 2 minutes on the 60-second test.  
• Finish with the “If you receive…” list.  
• Leave room for Q&A.

────────────────────────────────────────  
Handout tip  
Print the six red‑flags checklist on one page and the three fake email subject lines on the back—staff can take it home and use it as a quick cheat-sheet.
